intro: Every snippet below is copied from OpenClaw's actual source under C:\APPS\OC. They trace the real spine of the system: the gateway capability contract (TOOLS.md), the orchestrator's permission firewall, the LLM router every agent shares, and each specialist's core logic.

snippets.title: How a capability is wired — text, not code
snippets.feature: Capabilities wired as text, not code
snippets.code:
The OpenClaw npm package runs a gateway daemon as a systemd user
service. The gateway:
1. Polls Telegram getUpdates for the bot
2. Forwards each message to the active agent (default: main = Tasuke,
   model ollama/gemma4:26b)
3. The agent reads its workspace files on every turn — IDENTITY.md,
   SOUL.md, USER.md, MEMORY.md, and **TOOLS.md**
4. TOOLS.md lists "Conversation flows" — natural-language patterns
   mapped to shell commands.

This means wiring a new capability != writing a bot or webhook. It is:
> add a section to TOOLS.md -> restart the gateway -> the LLM uses it.
snippets.explanation: This is the single most important fact about OpenClaw. The gateway LLM re-reads TOOLS.md on every turn, so a capability is declared in Markdown and activated by a restart — no deploy, no webhook, no parallel bot. The canonical copy lives in the repo so it can be re-applied after an upgrade overwrites the live file.

snippets.title: Restart the gateway after editing flows
snippets.code:
systemctl --user restart openclaw-gateway.service
sleep 3 && curl -s http://127.0.0.1:18789/health
snippets.explanation: The gateway is a systemd --user service inside WSL. After editing TOOLS.md you restart it and probe the health endpoint on the gateway's TCP port 18789. Config changes hot-reload the worker; flow changes need this restart.

snippets.title: Three permission tiers
snippets.code:
TALK    — anyone in an allowed chat can trigger Tasuke to engage
            conversationally, deliver the public news briefing,
            translate it, and send a voice version.

  DO      — only RENNE (sender.id == 260811037) can ask Tasuke to
            mutate state: add/remove groups, schedules, friendly
            bots, news sites; change voice or language preferences.

  PRIVATE — personal information (calendar, inbox, bills, system
            health, file paths, secrets) is NEVER revealed in a
            non-DM chat. The firewall applies regardless of who asks.
snippets.explanation: The security model is three tiers enforced by the LLM on every message. TALK is open to anyone in an allowed chat; DO (state changes) is locked to the owner's exact Telegram user id; PRIVATE is an orthogonal rule that blocks personal info in group chats even for the owner. This is what makes it safe to add Tasuke to shared groups.

snippets.title: First-match gate evaluation
snippets.code:
## Gate evaluation order — FIRST MATCH WINS

### Gate 2: Is the sender the owner?
  sender.id == 260811037
    -> RENNE — full TALK and DO. PRIVATE rules still apply.

### Gate 3: Is the sender a bot (any bot)?
  sender.is_bot == true
    -> 1. Loop guard pre-check (bot-loop-guard.py check ...)
       2. If in friendly-bots.json -> known sibling (warmer tone)
       4. TALK actions only — never execute DO actions for a bot.
snippets.explanation:
Gates are evaluated top-down, first match wins. The owner is identified by a hard-coded user id (gate 2); other bots are routed through the loop guard and treated as TALK-only peers (gate 3). This ordered evaluation is the runtime contract the LLM follows for every inbound message.  

_Note: this excerpt is sanitised — identifiers naming the owner have been replaced with a generic term, per the project rule that no real person's name appears in documentation. The underlying source is unchanged._

snippets.title: Provider selection with automatic fallback
snippets.explanation: Every agent that needs an LLM routes through this one function. It reads KAZE_LLM_PROVIDER, tries the primary, and on any failure logs to stderr and falls back to the other provider. This is why a Cloudflare free-tier outage never takes the system down — local Ollama silently takes over.

snippets.title: think=false so reasoning models actually answer
snippets.code:
payload = json.dumps({
    "model": model,
    "prompt": prompt,
    "stream": False,
    "think": False,
    "options": {"temperature": temperature, "num_ctx": 8192,
                "num_predict": max_tokens}
}).encode()
...
text = result.get("response", "")
# Strip any residual think tags as a safety net
text = re.sub(r"<think>.*?</think>", "", text, flags=re.DOTALL).strip()
snippets.explanation: Reasoning models (qwen3, deepseek-r1) put output in a 'thinking' field unless think=false, which would leave the response empty. The router forces think=false and, belt-and-braces, strips any leftover <think> tags from the text — a hard-won gotcha applied consistently across the ecosystem.

snippets.title: Cloudflare Workers AI call
snippets.explanation: The free-tier cloud path: a plain stdlib urllib POST to Cloudflare Workers AI using the chat 'messages' shape, default model @cf/meta/llama-3.1-8b-instruct. No SDK, no key in code — credentials come from ~/.openclaw/secrets/kaze-llm.env.

snippets.title: Parallel RSS fetch with feedparser
snippets.code:
import feedparser
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor, as_completed
from difflib import SequenceMatcher

MAX_ITEMS_PER_FEED = 6
MAX_ITEMS_PER_CATEGORY = 12
FETCH_WORKERS = 8

def load_feeds():
    """Load the RSS feed definitions from kaze-feeds.json."""
    return load_json(FEEDS_PATH)["categories"]
snippets.explanation: Kaze fetches many feeds concurrently (8 workers), caps items per feed and per category, and uses difflib.SequenceMatcher to fuzzy-match near-duplicate titles so the digest does not repeat the same story from five outlets. Feeds and categories are pure config in kaze-feeds.json.

snippets.title: HTML cleaning for digest text
snippets.code:
def clean_text(text):
    """Strip HTML tags, collapse whitespace, and unescape entities."""
    text = text or ""
    text = html.unescape(text)
    text = re.sub(r"<[^>]+>", " ", text)
    text = re.sub(r"\s+", " ", text).strip()
    return text
snippets.explanation: RSS summaries arrive full of HTML and entities. This normaliser unescapes entities, strips tags, and collapses whitespace before the text is handed to the LLM for summarisation — keeping prompts clean and token-efficient.

snippets.title: Route a command, then execute the delegated shell
snippets.code:
def handle_text_command(tg, text): routed = run_router(text) response = routed.get("response", "(no response)") if not routed.get("execute"): tg.send_message(response) return tg.send_action("typing") tg.send_message(response) stdout, stderr, rc = run_shell(routed["execute"]) body = f"
{stdout.strip()[:3500]}
" if rc == 0 else \ f"⚠️ {routed['command']} failed (exit {rc})" tg.send_message(body)
snippets.explanation: The dispatch pattern (used by the fallback poller and mirrored by the live gateway flows): the router returns a response plus an optional 'execute' shell command. Tasuke acknowledges, runs the delegated agent script, and returns its output. This is the orchestrator-delegates-to-specialist mechanic in code.

snippets.title: Delegating /email to Yubin
snippets.explanation: Each command maps to a specialist agent and the exact shell to run. Tasuke never does the work itself — it names the agent ('yubin'), writes a user-facing line, and hands back the bash for the dispatcher to execute. Adding an agent is adding one of these mappings.

snippets.title: SQLite ledger initialisation
snippets.code:
DB_PATH = os.path.expanduser(os.environ.get(
    "KAKEI_DB", "~/.openclaw/workspace-kakei/kakei.db"))

def conn():
    os.makedirs(os.path.dirname(DB_PATH), exist_ok=True)
    c = sqlite3.connect(DB_PATH)
    c.row_factory = sqlite3.Row
    return c

def cmd_init(_args):
    with open(SCHEMA, encoding="utf-8") as f:
        c.executescript(f.read())
snippets.explanation: Kakei is the only agent with a database, and it is a single local SQLite file in its own workspace. init runs the committed schema (bills + expenses tables) idempotently. No central DB, no server — the ledger is a file you can back up by copying.

snippets.title: Weekly summary query
snippets.code:
bills = c.execute(
  """SELECT * FROM bills WHERE paid_at IS NULL
     AND due_date <= ? AND due_date >= ?
     ORDER BY due_date ASC""", (cutoff, today))
recent = c.execute(
  """SELECT category, SUM(amount) AS total, currency FROM expenses
     WHERE spent_on >= ? GROUP BY category, currency
     ORDER BY total DESC""", (week_ago,))
snippets.explanation: The Sunday rollup is two SQL queries: unpaid bills due in the window, and the week's spending grouped by category. The result is emitted as JSON and turned into a Telegram message. Kakei records only — there is no payment path by design.

snippets.title: Receipt photo -> ledger row
snippets.code: stdout, stderr, rc = run_shell( f"python3 {RECEIPT_SKILL} {shlex.quote(out)}", timeout=180) r = json.loads(stdout.strip()) tg.send_message( f"💰 Receipt logged.\n payee: {r['payee']}\n" f" amount: {r['amount']:.2f} {r['currency']}\n" f" ledger id: {r.get('expense_id')}")
snippets.explanation: Send a photo to Tasuke and it shells out to the receipt skill (OCR via qwen3-vl), which extracts payee/amount/date and inserts an expense row, then reports the new ledger id. The handler is built; the live gateway photo flow + qwen3-vl pull complete the loop (status: partial).

snippets.title: Local transcription pipeline
snippets.code:
Pipeline:
    1. ffmpeg converts the input to 16kHz mono 16-bit WAV
       (whisper.cpp requires this)
    2. whisper.cpp transcribes
    3. We strip whisper's bracketed timestamps and return plain text

def emit(status, **kwargs):
    print(json.dumps({"status": status, **kwargs}, ensure_ascii=False))
    sys.exit(0 if status == "ok" else 1)
snippets.explanation: Voice notes are transcribed entirely on-device: ffmpeg normalises the audio to the format whisper.cpp needs, whisper transcribes, timestamps are stripped. Nothing leaves the machine — the privacy guarantee Koe makes for spoken input.

snippets.title: Per-language neural voice selection
snippets.code:
DEFAULT_VOICES = {
    "pt": "pt-BR-FranciscaNeural",
    "en": "en-US-JennyNeural",
    "es": "es-ES-ElviraNeural",
    "ja": "ja-JP-NanamiNeural",
    "fr": "fr-FR-DeniseNeural",
}
snippets.explanation: Koe detects each paragraph's language and synthesises with the matching native (female) Microsoft neural voice via edge-tts, concatenating mixed-language input into a single Ogg/Opus file. edge-tts is free and keyless; Piper is the offline fallback.

snippets.title: Deterministic gateway + Ollama probe
snippets.code:
# Gateway
if ss -tlnp 2>/dev/null | grep -q ":18789"; then
  GW_STATUS="running"
else
  GW_STATUS="DOWN"
fi

# Ollama
if curl -s --max-time 5 http://127.0.0.1:11434/api/tags >/dev/null 2>&1; then
  OLLAMA_STATUS="running"
else
  OLLAMA_STATUS="DOWN"
fi
snippets.explanation: Sentry is deliberately LLM-free: pure shell checks that the gateway is listening on 18789 and Ollama answers on 11434. Determinism matters for a monitor — it must never hallucinate that a down service is up.

snippets.title: Severity verdict + dashboard JSON
snippets.code:
[ "$GW_STATUS" = "DOWN" ] && CRITICAL=$((CRITICAL+1))
[ "$OLLAMA_STATUS" = "DOWN" ] && WARNINGS=$((WARNINGS+1))
[ "$CONFIG_OK" = "false" ] && CRITICAL=$((CRITICAL+1))

if [ $CRITICAL -gt 0 ]; then VERDICT="🔴 CRITICAL ISSUES FOUND"
elif [ $WARNINGS -gt 0 ]; then VERDICT="🟡 WARNINGS"
else VERDICT="🟢 ALL CLEAR"; fi
snippets.explanation: Findings are scored into critical/warning counts that collapse to a single traffic-light verdict, written to both a human report and a dashboard JSON (sentry-latest.json). The gateway being down or the config being invalid are criticals; Ollama down is a warning (Cloudflare can cover).

snippets.title: HMAC-signed cross-bot messages
snippets.code:
# Telegram refuses to deliver messages between bots. This bridge
# fixes that: when one bot replies in a shared chat, peer-bridge.py
# POSTs the message to the other bot's endpoint with HMAC auth.
#
#   X-Peer-Bridge-Signature: hex(hmac_sha256(secret, f"{ts}.{body}"))
#   Body: { "synthetic_update": { ... Telegram-shaped ... } }
snippets.explanation: Telegram drops bot-to-bot messages, which blocks Maia and Tasuke from talking. The peer bridge sends an HMAC-signed HTTP POST carrying a synthetic Telegram-shaped update, so the receiving bot can route it through its normal pipeline. This is the candidate transport for the future Maia-OpenClaw marriage.

snippets.title: Loop guard against bot-war spirals
snippets.code:
# Maintains a per-chat counter and refuses if the chat exceeds the
# threshold of bot-to-bot exchanges within the cooldown window.
#
# Counter reset: ANY message from a human resets the counter to zero.
#
#   bot-loop-guard.py check --chat-id <id> --sender-is-bot <bool>
#       -> exits 0 if Tasuke MAY reply, 1 if it must stay silent
snippets.explanation: Two bots replying to each other would loop forever. Before answering a friendly bot, Tasuke calls the loop guard; if too many bot-only exchanges have happened in the window, it stays silent. A human speaking resets the counter — that signals the bot chatter is welcome again.

snippets.title: Querying the QI Hive Brain
snippets.code:
BRAIN_URL = os.environ.get("QI_BRAIN_URL", "http://localhost:9011").rstrip("/")
# Note: Brain API moved 9010 -> 9011 on 2026-05-14
#       (Logitech G HUB squats 9010).

def fmt_status():
    snap = call("/api/ecosystem_snapshot")
    if "_error" in snap:
        h = call("/health")  # fallback probe
    projects = snap.get("projects") or snap.get("project_states") or []
snippets.explanation: Tasuke reaches into the wider QI ecosystem by calling the QI Hive Brain at :9011 for status, project state, pending features, or a semantic 'ask'. It degrades to /health if the snapshot endpoint is missing, and never lets an exception leak to the user — failures become a short text line.
